The way in which the theatre disdained by White is made a base of operations by his opponent makes the game of fundamental interest to the student.
The answer to P-KKt4 would have been Kt—B3. Black wants to be attacked on the King's side, since he regards that theatre as unavailable. See note to move 12.

What sense can there be in this move? If in the end PxQP is played, then the answer BPxP would attain nothing other than the exposure of his own base Q3. Black then in this case would have worked for his opponent, for (let us suppose Black's P still at QB2) the strategic advance indicated for White, namely P-QB5xQP, would, after PxP, lead to exactly the same pawn configuration, and that the one which is the object of White's efforts!

This calculation contains, however, two logical errors. Firstly White in advancing P-QB5 will certainly not content himself with PxQP; this is only one threat. The insertion of a wedge (in other words the transference of the attack by P-QB6 would be by long odds the sharper threat. Secondly, White by B-QKt2, Kt-K2—KKt3, etc., has been untrue to his Queen's wing; the just punishment will lie in Black's becoming strong there!

A very difficult move. The answer to 18. ....PxP could be 19. KPxP, and Black, it is true, would get by 19. ....P-KB4; 20. KtPxP, PxP, two powerful pawns; but after 21. K-R1, and 22. R-KKt1, Black would stand badly; the mobility of his KP and KBP would in fact prove to be illusory, whereas White's King's side attack would be a very real one. Black intends to play PxQP at a moment when KPxP is not feasible.

Since P—KR4 has still further weakened White's position (the point KKt4), 20. ....PxP seems to be in place. The answer to 21. KPxP would have been Kt—KB3 as in the game; moreover, the threat to break through by P—QKt4 would be in the air.
The White Q goes in danger of her life. For instance 24. P—B4?, Kt—Kt1; If White had played 23. Kt—Kt5 then 23. ....Q-Q2; 24. P—B3, R—QB1, and the B threatens danger to her at KB1.

A clever resource, which is extraordinarily difficult to parry. Observe, too, that in the position now arrived at it looks for all the world as if White had all the time exclusively operated on the Queen's wing (by P-QB4—B5xQP, on which PxP had followed), whereas Black had sought salvation by a counter-attack directed against the base of the pawn-chain, White's PK4.
31. ....RxQKtP would have been answered by 32. RxKt. The sacrifice of the exchange is very promising.

This pawn sacrifice yields Black freedom to manoeuvre; without this sacrifices at Q6 or K5 would have been possible for White. Take for instance, the following variations: 33. ....Kt—K3 (instead of the text move); 34. P-QR4, B-Q1; 35. B-R3, Q-KB2; 36. BxP!, QxKt; 37. BxP ch, Kt—Kt2; 38. QxQ followed by 39. P-B7.
For now BxP, QxKt, BxP ch would be answered simply by K—R2.
Black has also his 33rd move to thank for the possibility of the Kt's intervention.
44. Resigns for Black will take the KP with a check and then the QKtP.
The exchange BxKt was to be considered.
In the long run something must be done for the QBP.
We have now got our pawn chain, and the Black base, the PQ3, already seems exposed (from the side), just as if the typical attack had been made on it by P-QB4-B5xQP, BPxP.
The Kt is already being sent forward to the attack of the exposed base.
To safeguard the Kt position at Qb4.

In this and similar positions the question arises, which pawn is the weaker, White's QKtP or Black's QRP? In the present case this problem could be solved by logical deduction. Since Black's PQ3 is weaker than White's PQ5, a like relation must exist throughout what remains of the Queen's wing. Were this not the case then White's P—QR4 must have been wrong, and that is unlikely. Was he in fact not justified in supporting his own important KtQB4? But that would be absurd. No, Kt-QB4 was indicated, similarly P-QR4; hence P-QKt4 must have led to a less favourable position for Black. And the course of the game proves the correctness of this judgment.
Kt-QB1 would perhaps have been better.
If Black could manage to play P-KB4, his position would not be so bad. But this is out of the question, and Black is besieged.
The masterly and varied uses made of the points Q2 and QB4 will be noted.

The rest of the game, which consists of bringing the K to the centre followed by an advance in close order of the fighting unit B, Kt and K is easily intelligible. There followed 34. ....B-K2; 35. K-B2, K-B2; 36. K-K2, K—K1; 37. K-Q3, K-Q2; 38. IC-B3, B-Qi; 39. Kt-B4 (QB3 is our shelter), 39. ....B—B2; 40. P—KKt4, B—Q1; 41. R-R6, B—B2; 42. P-KR4, B-Qi; 43. P-R5, B-B2; 44. P-QKt4, R-Kt2; 45. R-R8, K-Q1; 46. K-Kt3, R Kt1; 47. RxR, BxR; 48. P-QKt5, Kt-K2; 49. P—Kt6, P—KB4; (there is nothing left to hope for) 50. KtPxP, Kt-Kt1; 51. B-B2, Kt-B3; 52. B-R4 Resigns.
In the following game the transference of the attack from one point to another is carried out in classical style.
Hardly in place; better was R-K1 or P-KR3.
P-B3 would be answered by B-Q3.
No one knows better than Maroczy how to prevent freeing moves (here P-B5).
Threatens Kt—Kt6 and thus gains time for P—KKt5.
To exchange would make it more difficult to break through.
Only now does play begin on the real theatre. The idea is naturally attack on the base (PQB3) by P—QKt5.
Stops all attempts to break through by P-K4.

With this White transfers the attack to the new base, the PQKt2. Play against the base PQB3 could have been pursued by 29. Kt—Kt4 followed by say Q-R3—R4; but the transference of the attack to Black's QKt2 is still stronger, and above all safer. Süchting is now helpless.
The only way of saving the QKtP, otherwise there would have come Kt-R5, KtxKtP; and if RxKt, B-R6.
Our sacrificing advance of the unblockaded passed pawn. The pieces to the rear come to life. (See I. iv, § 2a)
and White won 39. K—K1, Kt—K3; 40. Q-K5, R-K1; 41. KtxKtP, Q-Kt6; 42. B-K2, Q-Kt8 ch; 43. K-B2; Q-KR8; 44. Kt-Q6, Q-R5 ch; 45. K-Kt2, KtxP ch; 46. QxKt, B-Q4 ch; 47. B-B3, BxB ch; 48. KxB Resigns.
Illustrates the idea of collective mobility, and touches also on the problem of prophylactic.
blocks.html: Illustrates the idea of collective mobility, and touches also on the problem of prophylactic.

blocks.text: A new idea. Black avoids developing the Kt at QB3, since it might be pinned by B-QKt5.

B-Q3 was much better here than the text move, firstly with regard to his development, and secondly because White threatens to make strong use of the diagonal QKt2 to KKt7, taking advantage of it to support his outpost at K5. A prophylactic measure was urgently needed. For instance 6. ....B-Q3!; 7. KtxKt, BxKt; 8. BxB ch, QxB; 9. BxKt, PxB; and the doubled pawn has both its dark and its bright side. (See II. ii.) Further we consider 6. ....B—K2 also better than the text move (P-QR3).
An admission of weakness in the long diagonal. There came under consideration also 9. ....B-Q3, e.g., 9. ....B-Q3; 10. Q-Kt4, Q-B2, followed by O-O-O.
The threat was 11. PxP, PxP; 12. Q-R5 ch, followed by QxQP.

The best place for the Q and one difficult to find. P—K4 would now only surrender the point Q4 to White. For instance 14. ....P K4; 15. Q-Kt3 (threatening BxP), B-Kt2; 16. P-K4, followed by P-Q3 and Kt—QB3-Q5 with advantage in position for White.

White plans the configuration PK4, PKB4, etc., which would leave his QP backward. As he thus sacrifices the effective power of his QP, he must necessarily first paralyse the three Black Q side pawns. Hence the text move.
A 'pawn roller' which can hardly be rendered innocuous.

If Black does nothing, White has the choice between a direct attack on the one hand and play against the QBP on the other. The latter could be carried out in some such way as say 19. ....QR—K1; 20. Q-K3 and then P-R5 and B-R3, finally driving away the defending BQ3 by P-K5. After the text move a mating attack wins the game straight off.

The following variation may be dedicated to those who love combinative 'complications. 21. Kt-Q5 (instead of P—K5), QxP; 22. QR—K1, QxQBP; 23. Kt-K7 ch, BxKt; 24. RxB, R-B2; 25. RxR, QxR; 26. Q-QB3, K-B1!; and Black, it would appear, has a sufficient defence.

If on his 21st move Black had played his B back to QKt1, he would now have been able to answer the entry of the Kt by Q-K3; but this, too, would have availed nothing. For example; 21. ....B-Kt1; 22. Kt-Q5. Q-K3; 23. Kt-B6 ch, RxKt; 24. PxR, Q-K5 (his one chance); 25. P-B7 ch, and White wins by 25. ....KxP; 26. QxRP ch; K—B1; 27. Q-Kt7 ch, K-K1; 28. R-K1, etc.
For if QxQP, Q-R6 forces mate, or the loss of a R, and if 24. ....Q-K2, the fatal Q shows herself at her QB3 and there is no answer.

The following game shows how easily the early surrender of the centre can lead to disaster. Nevertheless, this procedure seems to us to be in itself quite practicable, provided we bring to bear on the problem all the tenacity which we possess, and do not allow ourselves to be forced down an inclined plane.

If we do this our prospects for the future are good. As examples we may point to Rubinstein's games of this kind which he won at St. Sebastian in 1911, and further to Game No. 28 in this book. We now proceed to
Gives up the centre, but opens the Q file and the long diagonal QKt2 to KR8 for pressure on White's centre.
Better would be P-QKt3, but the text move is playable.
If. 8. B-KKt5, B-K2; 9. BxKt, then best 9. ....PxKt.

The tenacity of purpose so necessary to tournament play fails him here. Why not Q-Q4? If then 13. P-QB4, Q-QR4 followed presently by QR-Q1; and the pressure is already sensible. If, however, 13. P-QB4, Q-QR4; 14. P-Q5, then 14. ....QR-K1!, with strong counter-threats. For instance 15. PxP?, BxKt; followed by QxB., Why the mere contact with the point Q4 must bring a blessing is evident. This point in the first place is the outpost station in the Q file, and in the second the same thing in the diagonal QKt2 to KR8, while lastly, Q4 is a blockading point. The enormous strategical importance to Black of the point Q4 makes it clear that any, the most passing, Contact with it must work wonders.
Now this move is unfavourable, since the QBP is in the air. The inclined plane makes its appearance.
15. ....QR-QB1 was to be considered here, and after 16. B—K5, KR—Q1, the advance of White's pawn majority is very much hindered.
Black will not resign himself to the loss of a pawn, runs risks in seeking compensation, and thus loses the Queen.
With 16. ....KR-QB1; 17. B-K5, Kt-Q2! (with a view to the threatened K-R1 and R-KKt1), he could still have put up a resistance.
For if now 18. B-K4, then 18. ....KtxB; 19. BxR, Kt-Kt3, and Black threatens Kt-B5 with later B-Q3 and Q-KR4.

In a situation very similar to that in the preceding game Tartakower succeeds in making the point Q4, which Mieses so badly neglected, the basis of an undertaking which he carried out with great virtuosity.
blocks.html: In a situation very similar to that in the preceding game Tartakower succeeds in making the point Q4, which Mieses so badly neglected, the basis of an undertaking which he carried out with great virtuosity.

blocks.text: The best answer to 5. Kt-QB3 would be 5. ....Kt-Q2, and the proud KtK5 will be forced to declare his intentions.
Threatening both QxKtP and QKt5 ch.
He does not hesitate at employing the Rook to protect the modest pawn!

Both sides have now completed their development, and the game is about equal. But White's centre, which is otherwise well protected, betrays a striking measure of immobility. My System, however, teaches that every immobile complex tends to become a weakness. The truth of the proposition will here be shortly manifested.
He feels himself here as if at home, for P-K4 is not possible because of KtxQP.

If 13. Kt—K4, the result would be the mobilization of Black's Q side by 13. ....P-QKt4; 14. Kt K5, KtxKt; 15. PxKt, P-QB4; 16. P-QP3, P-QB5, etc.; or 14. Kt-Q2, P-K4, etc. and White's game is disorganized.
White's centre is already being demolished.
He makes use of the point Q4 in excellent fashion.
Black has a decided advantage for the end game. Pawn majority on the Q side, the Q file, and last but not least the central position of his Q. This advantage is, however, still only a small one.

Centralization proceeds apace! White's pawn majority is much less easily realizable than Black's (if for instance 26. P-KB3, than 15. ....P-KB4, and White's K4 is in bondage), and this is sufficient to explain the loss of the game.
The whole ending is played by Tartakower with wonderful precision and truly artistic elegance. Tartakower is, in my opinion, without question the third best end game artist of all living masters.
Only now, and this tardiness is to his credit, does he give up the central position in favour of a diversion.
In order on 37. Q-K1 to put in operation the following manoeuvre: 37. ....Q-B4 ch; 38. K-K4, Q-KB4 ch. followed by Q-QB7 and wins.
White is already at his last gasp.
The following game illustrates the plan of action 'centre file's attack on a flank'.

White has now the attacking position in the centre. This is unquestionably an advantage. But here the weakness of his PK4 (we shall quickly see why K4 is weak) will soon force White to surrender this advantage; that is to say he will find himself obliged to equalize with PxKP.
In order to exchange the B.

Since the B is needed at Q3 for the protection of the KP, the QP can only be protected against a Kt at K3 by exchanging him. The student should consider carefully the motif here used, aimed at forcing the opponent to declare himself (whether for PxP or for P-Q5).

With this and the next move a diversion is put en train which maybe said to run counter to the spirit of the opening. The right line of play consisted in B-K3 and the doubling of the R's in the Q file. By this means advantage could have been taken of the rather uncomfortable position of White's BQ3. Black's simplest course would have been to play B-K3 on his 14th move.
The entry of the Kt at KB5 would, according to my analysis, have decided the game in White's favour. See the Diagram.

The retreat of the Black Kt at R6 is cut off. The attempt at a rescue undertaken by means of a reckless advance of the K side pawns gives opportunity, often occurring in such a position, for a decisive counter stroke, by an invasion in the centre, in the present case by Kt-B5.

For instance 22. Kt-B5, PxP; 23. PxP, BxKt; 24. PxB, Kt—K2; 25. K—Kt2, K-Kt2 (is the P sacrifice 25. ....P—Kt5; 26. PxP, Kt-Kt4 any better?); 26. KxKt, R-KR1 ch (or 26. ....Kt-Q4; 27. Q-K2); 27. K-Kt2, Q-R3; 28. K-B2, Q-R7 ch; 29. Kt—Kt2, R-R6; 30. K—K1, RxP; 31. Kt—K3, etc. Moreover, as a superabundance, 26. R-KR1 is also playable, which I showed to be a win for White in an analysis I published in the Rigaer Rundschau.

Now the Kt rejoices in his rediscovered freedom, and Black, after this doubtful excursion, which could easily have ended fatally for him, takes up the right line, play in the Q file, and pursues it with complete mastery to victory. What remains needs but few remarks. The continuation was: 23. R-B2, KtxB; 24. KtxKt, B-K3; 25. QR-Q1, KR-Q1; 26. P-QKt3, Kt-B5; 27. Kt-Kt2, KtxKt (Q3); 28. RxKt, RxR; 29. QxR, R-Q1 (why not BxKKtP?); 30. Q-K2, P-R6; 31. Kt—K3, P-QR4; 32. R-B1, P-R5; 33. P-QB4, R-Q5!; 34. Kt-QB2, R-Q2; 35. Kt—K3, Q-Q1; 36. R-Q1, RxR; 37. KtxR, Q-Q5 (Q file and centralization); 38. Kt—B2, P-QKt4!; 39. BPxP, RPxP; 40. RPxP, BxQKtP (threatening Q-R8 ch); 41. KtxP, B-Q8; 42. Q-KB1, PxP; 43. K-Kt2, P-Kt5; 44. Q-Kt5, P-Kt6; 45. Q-K8 ch, K-Kt2; 46. Q-K7, P-Kt7; 47. KtxP, B-Kt6 and wins.
The next game illustrates the plan of action: play in a file against the enemy centre: First restrain, then blockade, and lastly destroy!

It would be more in the spirit of a correct attack on a pawn-chain first to play 9. ....PxP; 10. KtxP, and not till then P-KB3. But after 10. ....P-KB3; 11. PxKBP, QxP; the position arrived at is after all similar to that of the text.
The diagonal attacking range KKt2 to Q5 is a necessary element in White's plan of operations; for this, after KPxBP, holds up the freeing thrust P-K4 better than any other possible disposition could.

Bravo! The flank attack KtxKtP has no terrors for him, since a flank attack by itself can never ruin a strongly centralized game. And White's game is centralized, for he holds the centre files and pressure in them is already making itself felt, and further he has the prospect of occupying the central points Q4 and K5. Observe now how Black's wing attack is thrown back by action in the centre.
There will come a Rook presently to gobble up the QBP.
If 19. ....B-Q2, then 20. KtxKP, BxKt; 21. RxB, followed by BxQP.
Now he has a go on the other wing.

It would have pleased me even better if the decision had been brought about in a Bishop ending instead of through the somewhat 'tacked on' action of the passed PQB7; for instance from such a position as White: K, K5; B, KR3; P's, QR2, QB3, KB4, KR2. Black: K, K2; B, KB2; P's, QR3, Q4, K3, KR2; with the continuation P—KB5, PxP; BxP, and White wins the QP and the game. We should then have the general idea more markedly brought out, namely first to keep the KP and QP under restraint, then to blockade them and only at the end to destroy them. But as played the game was instructive enough! (e.g., Moves 13, 16 and 18).
The following game is instructive for the way in which Black turns his majority in the centre to account despite disturbing counter-measures.
Since P-K5 did not seem to be dangerous.
There was also to be considered 4. Kt-B3, Kt-QB3; 5. P-Q4, PxP; 6. KtxP, B-Kt5; 7. Q-Q3 (Bugoljubow's suggestion).

An interesting idea. He, so to speak, sacrifices a P, in that he makes his pawn majority on the Q side of no value; but he hopes, by occupying certain central points, to be able to bring counter-pressure to bear. Cf. the next note.
White's-command of the diagonal KKt2 to QKt7 coupled with that of the point K4 is no small embarrassment to Black. If now 10. ....Q-K4 ch?, then 11. Kt—K4 and B-KB4.
Not 12. ....P—KB4 because of the reply 13. B-B3 followed by Kt-Q2 and Black's K4 will remain a weak point.

An ingenious move, which, however, brings about a disturbance of the equilibrium which up to now may be said to have existed. Better was 14. P-KB4!, Kt-Q2; 15. B-Q2, K—R1!; 16. QR-K1, Kt-B3; 17. B-QB1. After the text move the balance weighs in Black's favour.
Otherwise B-B4, and the balance is readjusted.
The game is already lost for White, for the occupation of the point K4 which seems to consolidate the position proves to be deceptive. White's KKt3 is in fact sick unto death.
24. RxP, RxKtP ch; 25. K-B2, Kt—K4 would lead to a debacle.
Or 25. K-B2, Kt-K4; 26. K-K2, RKt7 ch; 27. K-B1, R-Kt6 winning a piece.
If 27. P—Kt6 ch then, best, K-B3 (not K—K2 because of 28. Kt—R2, R-KR1; 29. R-K2, R(Kt)-R5??; 30. B-Kt5 ch).
In which seven White pawns show greater collective mobility than eight Black ones. Thus does mind (i.e., dynamic effect) triumph over mere matter.
blocks.html: In which seven White pawns show greater collective mobility than eight Black ones. Thus does mind (i.e., dynamic effect) triumph over mere matter.

blocks.text: The collective mobility of White's King's side pawns already makes itself quickly felt.
In order to provoke P-QR3, after which the lack of protection under which the QKtP will suffer is to form the basis of a sharp combination.
Else there would follow QR-Q1 and P-Q4 with advantage to White.
or PxKt; BxQKtP. Cf. the note to White's 9th move.
White has succeeded in wresting the long diagonal from his opponent.

The connexion between 'sacrifice' and ' blockade' would have stood out in even sharper relief had the continuation been 19. P-KB5, P—KKt4, 20, P—KR4 with an enduring attack, while Black's pawn plus would have but an illusory value.

In the following game we have an example of a 'mysterious' Rook move, also a striking one of the difference between a true and a false freeing move. As this game in addition illustrates very clearly our conception of prophylactic strategy, it is inserted here.

The best move, for the early development of the Kt's advocated by Lasker would not get at the root of the matter here. This root lies rather in the pawn configuration and in the prevention of any freeing pawn moves.

Black plays (as will become evident in his 8th move) to prevent the advance of the QP to his fourth which would in a certain sense have a freeing effect; since it would make White's majority in the centre felt. Black, as he plays it, succeeds in completely crippling the enemy majority in the centre. And now the reader may ask, why does Black give White the opportunity of playing P-Q4 on his 7th move?

White forgoes the advance, and rightly, for 7. P-Q4 would here be the typical false liberating move, which merely creates new weaknesses. E.g., 7. P-Q4, Kt-Q2!; 8. P-Q5 (otherwise ultimately KPxQP with play against White's isolated KP), 8. ....B-KB2 followed by the occupation of the point PB4 by B or Kt.
With the aid of the resources he has in the Q file Black now succeed! in forcing his opponent to act on the defensive. See Black's 9th and 10th moves.
The reward which Black's systematic scheme of operations has earned for him. White's PQ3 is now a weakness.

The 'mysterious' Rook move, which in the event of White playing P-Q4 threatens to make things uncomfortable for him in the K file. In addition to this it makes room for the B at KB1 to which square the latter wishes to go.

White has made pertinent use of the open KB file, his one advantage. Black's move for all its unpretentiousness has its significance in position play. Black insures the eventual possibility of playing P-KKt3 and P-KB4 without being disturbed by a check at R6.
Renders possible a parry to the ever threatening advance P-KKt5. For example: 18. P—Kt5, P-KKt3; 19. Kt-Kt3, P-KB4!; with an excellent game. Cf. the previous note.
White's QRP is constantly threatened, and if P-QKt3, P-R5 will now be possible. It is evident that White's Q wing is sympathetically affected by the weakness of his centre.

B-Kt6 would have been a strong move here, although by it Black would have to forgo this parry he had planned to P-KKt5. Nevertheless, B-Kt6 could have composedly been played (one should not be a slave to one's parries!), e.g., 19. ....B-Kt6; 20. P—KKt5, PxP; 21. BxP, P-QB5! (Lasker's suggestion); 22. PxP, Q-K3; 23. Kt-K3, Q-KKt3; 24. Q-Kt4, B-QB4!, and wins. Or 23. Q-KB3!, BxP; 24. KR-Q1, and Black has a slight advantage.
Some tempi could have been saved by playing P-QKt5 at once.
Black ought now to play out his trumps.

Black had brought about a strategically won position, only he should not have delayed any longer playing out his trumps. These consisted of Kt-Q5, which would lead to BxKt, and of P-KKt3 and B-R3, in order to dominate the diagonal. Thus:

BxKt, BPxB, followed by B-R3. Or 25. Q-Q1 (instead of exchanging), R-QR1, followed by Q-QR5; the exchange of Q's will be forced and Black has a good. end-game. He could also play out his trumps in the reverse order; e.g., 23. ....Kt—Q5; 24. BxKt, BPxB; 25. Q-B3 (best), P—KKt3; 26. Kt—Kt3, Q-K2; 27. Kt-Q1, B-R3; 28. R—KKt2, B-Kt4! followed by R—QR1—R8, etc.
There was still time for Kt-Q5, etc.
Thanks to a tactical sally (White's 26th move) this thrust which was thought to have been prevented, is now after all possible.
Robs Black of the fruits of his deep plan of campaign.
There followed 26. ....PxKt; 27. KtxBP, Kt-Q5; 28. Q-B2 (Q-R5 would have won quicker), Q—QB3; 29. KtxR, QxKt; 30. BxKt, KPxB; 3o. PxP, and won easily.

What we have to learn from this game is the ability to distinguish between true and false freeing moves. The manner in which Black was able to hold in check the thrusts P-Q4 and later (until the moment of aberration) P—KKt5 is worthy of special notice. See II. ii, § 3.
The following game illustrates the effect of preventive measures and the idea of collective mobility.
A novelty which at the price of a backward QP aims at securing other advantages.

It was not possible here to take immediate advantage of White's weakness at Q3. For instance, 6. ....Kt-Q6 ch; 7. K-K2!, Kt—B5 ch; 8. IC-B1, with the threat P-Q4. Or 6. ....Kt—Q6 ch; 7. K—K2, KtxB ch; 8. RxKt, Kt-QB3; 9. B-QKt5, B-Q2; 10. BxKt, followed by P-Q4 with the superior end-game.
I should prefer P-QR3 here, though it is true that even then White with 8. P-QR3, Kt-QB3; 9. PQ3 and BK3, would have an excellent game. See II. i. 4.

White now stands very well; any weakness at Q3, which may exist, is covered up, the collective mobility of White's K side (P-KB4!) is considerable, and, most important, the apparently blocked KB plays from the background a preventive role (directed against a possible P—K4) which goes far to turn the scale in White's favour.
Directed against the threat B-Kt5 ch, B-Q2; KtxP.
Q-Kt4 would have been very strong here; e.g., 12. Q-Kt4, O-O; 13. B-KKt5!, B-K2; 14. B-KR6, B-B3; 15. BxKtP, BxB; 16. Kt—R5; or else 13. ....P-K4;

14. Q—R4, with the sacrifice at Kt7 to follow (Kt—R5xKtP). The best answer to Q—Kt4 would have been P-KB3; for instance, 12. Q-Kt4, Q-B3; 13. P-KB4; but even in this case White's superiority in position would have been very great. After the less incisive text move Black can approximately equalize.

A direct mating attack is no longer feasible. For example: 13. P-K5, B-B2!; 14. Q-Kt4, K-R1; 15. Kt-R5, R-KKt1; 16. R-B3, P-KB4!; 17. PxP e.p., PxP; 18. Q-R4, R-Kt3; 19. R-R3, Q-K2; and Black threatens to consolidate his position by B-Q2 and QR-KKt1.
Rubinstein has defended himself skilfully, but White has always a trump in hand, the K file.

Not good. In cramped positions one should never give away any the slightest future possibility of a move. But Q-B2 gives away the possibility of playing Q-KB3, after PxP, PxP. The right move was therefore 16. ....BQ-2, and if then 17. PxP (best), PxP; 18. KR-K1, then 18. ....Q-B3, and Black stands much better at any rate than he does in the game.

The Kt starts on a long journey with KKt5 as his goal, in order to support with all the means at his disposal the KB who now wakes up and throws off his preventive role for one of direct activity. And meanwhile White's K file, thrown, so to speak, on its own resources, makes a desperate but successful struggle for existence. This vitality of the K file gives point to the Kt manoeuvre.
We see now that 21. ....R—K1 would be met by 22. Q-Q5.
And here 22. ....R—K1 would lead to a combination full of pleasantries, e.g., 22. ....R-K1; 23. Q-R5!, RxR; 24. Kt—Kt5, P-KR3; 25. Q-Kt6, PxKt; 26. Q-R5 mate.
Black's castled position was still too strongly defended, so White intends first to force a re-grouping of the enemy forces.
The switch-back theme, such as usually only occurs in problems. 27. Q—K1 would, however, also have been good, e.g., 27. Q-K1, B-K5; 28. Kt-B2, winning a P by KtxB, etc.
The answer to R-B3 would have been Kt-Kt5, P-KR3; Kt-R7 winning at once.

If 28. ....P-KR3 there would follow 29. P—KKt4 with a very strong attack. Thus: 29. P-Kt4, PxP; 30. P-B5, QxR; 31. P-B6 ch, QxP; 32. QxP mate. Or 29. P-Kt4, P-Kt4?; 30. PxKtP, threatening mate at R6. After the text move White forces an elegant win.
If 29. ....RxR; then 30. PxR, QxB; 31. Kt-Kt5, Q-Kt1; 32. P-K6, B-Q4; 33. Q-B4, with an easy win.
A remarkable position; Black is lost. In spite of the scanty material a mating attack is in the air. Some pretty play now follows.

If 32. ....K-B1, White wins by 33. Q-K5, B-Q1 (best; the reply to 33. ....QxP would be 34. Q-B6 ch, K-Kt1; 35. Kt-K6; or 34. ....B-B2; 35. KtxB and QxB); 34. Kt-K6 ch, K-K2; 35. Q-QB5 ch!, K-Q2; 36. Kt-B8 ch! Observe how White on his 35th move forgoes the discovered check and how the Black King has got tangled up with his own pieces.
If 34. ....PxP, then 35. Kt-K6, P-KR4!; 36. Q-B6 ch, K-R2; 37. Kt-Kt5 ch, K-R3; 38. B-Kt4 leads to a mate.
Illustrates the restraint of a double complex in an extraordinarily striking manner.
blocks.html: Illustrates the restraint of a double complex in an extraordinarily striking manner.

blocks.text: White: Nimzowitsch. Black: Marquis S. Rosselli del Turco.

We have here to do with the remarkable situation which we have already had occasion to notice (see II. ii, § 2 Diagram CXXXIII), namely the one in which we do not at once cause the doubled pawns by BxKt, PxB, but rather bring, this about by a roundabout way. As a fact after 8. BxKt ch?, PxB, we should never be able to force our obstinate opponent to accommodate us by playing P-Q5, e.g., 8. BxKt, PxB; 9. P-K4, Kt-KB3; etc.
Threatening Kt-B4, Q-B2; BxKt ch, PxB; and the weakness of the double pawn is evident.
The manoeuvre of the Q is intended to help prevent Black's castling on the Q side; not on the K side as one might at first sight think.
Not O-O-O because of Kt-R5 and the covering move KKt-K2 is ruled out because of QxBP.
Now she rejoices in the observation post she has won for herself. This Q manoeuvre has quite a hypermodern air to it.
Q-K6 ch, K-Q1 (or B-K2; Kt-R5); BxKt, and the unpleasant doubled pawn is a fact.
At the right moment, for the Q dare not retake. For instance, 16. ....QxB; 17. QxP, R-K1; 18. O-O!!, QxP (RxP; Kt-K5 ch); 19. Q-QB7 ch!! and wins (19. ....Q-K2; 20. Kt-Q6 ch followed by KtxR).
At last White has achieved his end, at the cost it is true of a P, but this here plays but a subordinate role.

For (see the previous note) Black's position can be broken up. (Obviously White must not allow Black to safeguard his position by Kt—K4.) To break up Black's game three pawn moves are necessary, i. P—QB3, ii. P-K5, and iii. P—KR4. If White contented himself with only two of these his work were but half done. In the game all three are brought about.
Now this R is happily tethered (to his PQ5).
If 21. ....PxP; then 22. PxP, KxP; 23. Q-K4, and Kt-Kt6 is impracticable on account of BxP ch
The reply to P—KB4 would have been Q-QKt1, an attacking move in the best modern spirit. For example, 22. ....P-B4; 23. Q-Kt1, K-K3 (to protect the KBP); 24. Q-Q3! and Kt-Q6! with a decisive attack.
Now the undermined Black position tumbles like a house of cards.
For after 25. ....B-Kt2; 26. Kt-K5 ch, BxKt; 27. QxB, Black's King is in his helplessness a pathetic figure.
Illustrates a position held under complete restraint, and may serve as a pendant to my game (No. 8 ) against Sämisch.
blocks.html: Illustrates a position held under complete restraint, and may serve as a pendant to my game (No. 8) against Sämisch.

blocks.text: Black intends to bring into existence the double complex only under conditions favourable to himself. Cf. No. 34.

The prognosis for the complex PQB2, PQB3, etc., is in a measure (but not pronouncedly) in favour of Black. Yet after e.g., 9. P-K4, P-K4; 10. P-Q5, Kt-QR4; Black Would not have bought the barricade which he has achieved altogether cheaply, for his QBP would then have been much better placed if it were still at QB2. (See the remarks on the double complex in II. ii, § 2 my game against Janowski; Diagram CXXXIII)
A fine idea. In reply to 9. ....P-K4; 10. P-Q5, Kt-QR4, the intention is by 11. Kt-Kt3 to bring the aggressive Black Kt at R4 to reason.
There was time enough for this. P-KB4 should first have been played.

follow 11. PxP, QPxP; 12. P-Q5, Kt-QR4; 13. Kt-Kt3, Kt-Kt2; 14. P—K4, Kt—K1, and the weak point QB4, which is now attackable also from Black's Q3, will be protected by Q-K2, while White for his part can use the KB file together with. P-QR4-R5 as a base of operations. The game would then stand about even.
For the reply to 11. P-Q5 would now be P-K5! Thus: 11. P-Q5, P-K5; 12. B-K2, Kt—K4!; or 12 PxKt, PxB; with advantage to Black.
11. ....Q-K2 was also possible, for if say 12. BPxP, QPxP; 13. P—Q5, then 13. ....Kt-Q1; 14. P-K4, Kt—K1; and Black by Kt-Q3 and P-KB3 gets a strong defensive position. (Cf. the note to move 10.)

Black sees in White's K side pawns (KB, KKt and KR) a qualitative majority. The text move involves a complicated system of restraint. A simpler one could have been brought about by 12. ....Kt—K1. For example: 12. ....Kt-K1; 13. P-KKt4 (or 13. P-KB5, Q-Kt4), 13. ....P-KB4; 14. QPxP! (observe the 'dead' B at QB1 and consider further how ineffectively posted the White pieces are for an attack to be launched in the KKt file). 14. ....QPxP; 15. Q-Q5 ch, QxQ; 16. PxQ, Kt—K2; 17. R-Q1, Kt-Q3; and Black has rather the better game.

If 14. B-Q2, Black would still get the advantage. For instance: 14. B-Q2 (to threaten B-K1-R4) 14. ....Kt-B4; 15. Q-K1 (best; Black threatened Kt—Kt6 and to exchange the B, when White's QB4 would become very weak), 15. ....P-KKt3; and if now 16. P-KKt4, Kt-Kt2; 17. Q-R4, then Kt(B)-K1, and the pawn movement is strangled at birth; for now would follow at the next move the powerful P—KB4. So we get always the same picture. The awkwardness of White's pieces as a result of the doubled pawns renders more difficult by far the carrying out of any action on the K side however this is planned.
Q-R4 will not do because of 15. ....Kt-B4; 16. Q-Kt5, Kt-R2; 17. QxRP, Kt—Kt6.

The Q is bound for—KR2! Where she will be excellently placed, for then the crippling of White's K side by P-R5 will at once be threatened. It must be conceded that the restraint manoeuvre Q-Q2-B4-R2 represents a remarkable conception.
Threatening Kt-Kt5 ch; PxKt, PxP ch; K-Kt1, P-Kt6; etc.
In this position the backwardness of the QKtP is easy to put up with.
Black wishes to force P-Q5 in order then to operate undisturbed on the K side.
Otherwise B-K3 would follow and P-Q5 would be forced after all.

And now comes the. attack. So was Q-Q2-B4—R2 actually an attacking manoeuvre? Yes and no. No, since its whole idea was to restrain White's K side pawns. Yes, since every restraining action is the logical prelude to an attack, and since every immobile complex tends to be a weakness and therefore must sooner or later become an object of attack.
White has very skilfully brought up all his defensive forces.
Opens the KKt file for himself, but the K file for his opponent. This move, therefore, demanded deep deliberation.

Seizes his chance. Black's KP now needs to be defended. If he had limited himself to purely defensive measures, as say 31. B-Q2, a pretty combination would have resulted; namely, 31. B-Q2, R—Kt3!; 32. B—K1, Kt-Kt5 ch; 33. PxKt, PxPch; 34. K-Kt2, BxP!; 35. QxB, and now follows the quiet move 35. ....P-K6; and Q-R6 mate can only be parried by KtxP, which move, however, would cost White his Q.

Here I had naturally expected Kt-Q2 for Black's obligation to defend the important KP furnished White's only counter chance, as has already been observed. But a result of that move would have been a delightful Q sacrifice, namely: 32. Kt-Q2, B-B1; 33. KtxP, Q-B4; 34. Kt-B2, QxRP ch; 35. KtxQ, Kt—Kt5 mate. The point, moreover, lies in the fact that the moves B-B1 and Q-B4 cannot be transposed. E.g., 32. Kt-Q2, Q-B4? (instead of B-B1); 33. Q-Q1!, B-B1; 34. Q-KB1, and everything is protected; whereas if 32. ....B-B1, 33. Q-Q1, the move BxRP! would wipe out the corner stone of White's building. (34. KxB, Q-B4 ch; etc.)
34. KxB, Q-B4 ch; 35. K-R2 would have led to mate in three.
Best, for P—KR5 can no longer be withstood. After the fall of White's KRP the defence is hopeless.

A precise finish, for now there is threatened 41. ....KtxR; 42. RxKt, Q-R8 ch; 43. K-K2, Q-R ch!; and against this threat White is defenceless. If 41. K-R1, then, 41. ....Kt-B6 ch; 42. K-B1 or Q1, Q-R8 ch would lead to mate.
One of the best blockading games that I have ever played.

blocks.html: Illustrates the isolated QP.

blocks.text: P-Q5 would be bad because of Kt-QR4; P-QKt3, B-QKt5; nor would 10. B-KKt5 be good, e.g., 10. ....P-QKt3, etc.
P-QR3 and P-QKt4 would unnecessarily weaken the point QB4.

A strategically noteworthy conception. White says to himself: in the centre I am strong, therefore a strategical diversion is justified; moreover, I have no particular wish after say 15. B-R6 or Q3 to be saddled with hanging pawns. The right move was, nevertheless, B-R6. For example: 15. B-R6, KtxKt; 16. PxKt, Q-B2; 17. BxB, QxB; 18. P-QB4 with eventually P-QR4-R5.

There was no occasion for this. There were other lines of play to be considered, (i) 19. ....P-QR4 and KR-QB1, or (ii) 19. ....KR-Q1 followed by Kt-Q2-KB1; for (iii) Kt—K1, see the remarks on Diagram CL in II. iii, § 4.
Weakens the point QB4. After 20. ....P-QR4 (instead of the text move) and KR-QB1, there would not be much wrong with him.
By occupying this outpost station White gets play in the QB file.

What now follows could serve as a text book example for play in an open file. The slowness with which White step by step gains in terrain is also of significance from the point of view of position play.
In order to relieve the KBP and to make Q-Kt4 possible.
Breaks down the opposition in the QB file.
If 29. ....Kt-K5; then 30. P-B6!, P—KKt4; 31. PxB, R-KB1; 32. R-B8 and wins.
The QBP, the fruit of the operations on the Q's file, now brings the decision.

Is dedicated to hanging pawns, and is characteristic of these though only in a quite special sense. It shows the frightful dangers to which hanging pawns are exposed at birth. Infant mortality is very high among them, and appreciably exceeds the mortality of grown up hanging pawns, who if the worst comes to the worst can seek refuge in 'blockaded security'.
blocks.html: Is dedicated to hanging pawns, and is characteristic of these though only in a quite special sense. It shows the frightful dangers to which hanging pawns are exposed at birth. Infant mortality is very high among them, and appreciably exceeds the mortality of grown up hanging pawns, who if the worst comes to the worst can seek refuge in 'blockaded security'.

blocks.text: P-QB4 is possible here. For instance, 7. ....P-QB4; 8. PxQP, KtxP; 9. BxB, QxB; 10. KtxKt, PxKt; 11. PxP, KtxP; and the isolani does not look so bad.

The correctness of this move stands or falls by that of the pawn sacrifice recommended in the next note. Sound and good is, instead of P-QB4, 12. ....R-QB1 as given by Dr. Lasker. For instance, 13. Q-Kt3, KtxKt ch, followed by P-QB4. Not quite so good, yet by no means bad would seem to be 12. ....P—KR3; 13. B-KB4, B-Q3; 14. BxB, PxB.

If then 14. PxP, KtxP, Black would have attacking chances; the answer to 14. Kt-Q4 could be Kt(Q2)xP. The outcome of the game would have been doubtful in either case, whereas now there is no doubt whatever. It may be observed that if 13. ....Kt(Q2)xP, then 14. KtxQP!, BxKt; 15. B-QB4 wins.
The gale has not only blown away the hanging pawns but has also taken a piece along with them. Black's desperation attack is warded off easily.
Lasker praises this move, but 21. Q—Q5 seems to do as well. E.g., 21. ....PxP; 22. QxKtP, Q-QB7; 23. B-B6! True, many roads lead to Rome.
If 24. ....R(Kt1)xP; then R—B8 ch! and wins outright.
There followed 26. B-K7, R-K1; 27. K-Kt1, R-K7; 28. BxP, R-Q1; 29. B-Q4, R-OBi; 30. R-KKt4, Resigns.
Took an instructive course. It was played in a simultaneous exhibition in Leipzig in 1926. White; Schurig with, up to the 12th move, K. Laue of Halle.
blocks.html: Took an instructive course. It was played in a simultaneous exhibition in Leipzig in 1926. White; Schurig with, up to the 12th move, K. Laue of Halle.

blocks.text: With the text move an original manoeuvre begins. Black plans an attack on the extreme Q's wing; but before launching it wishes to safeguard his centre against the possible threat of P-K4-K5; and accordingly first sees to the over-protection of his K4. Further, from where she stands his Q has at her disposal a reserve square in QKt1 to which she can withdraw if need arise, e.g., should the QB file be opened.

The question whether a flank attack is admissable or not can only be solved by reference to the actual position in the centre. If this be secure a flank attack cannot be wholly amiss. So, too, here. And what matters it that the K has not yet castled? As it is he is unassailable.
P-K4 seems more to the point.
A bit premature in my opinion.
Every free moment is used to the strengthening of the position on the extreme Q's wing.

This move must be credited to Black's strategy in over protecting his K4. The valuable diagonal QKt2 to KB6 is now obstructed; but by no other means could the thrust P-K5 have been effected. Those engaged in this over-protection have once more stood the test excellently. Moreover, they have had to put up with no inconveniences, but have made themselves felt in all directions.

One variation should be mentioned, namely 19. P-KB4 in order to keep the QP at Q3. The continuation might have been 19. ....B—B4 ch!, and White has after all to submit to playing 20. P-Q4, and after 20. ....B-B1; 21. P-K5 we should have arrived at the position in the text.
The White bishops have now small possibilities of action.
P-R6 at once would have been more precise.
It was essential to interpolate here B-KB1.
Black with the move forces his way into the enemy game by means of a sacrifice of the exchange, and wins the entrenched QRP. How does he do it?
This interesting combination should begin with Kt—B4 (not B—B4). The difference will soon be manifest.
The interpolation here of B-KB1 (which would, not have been possible if Black had played 23. ....Kt-B4) would have yielded him an extra tempo for the end game.
We can see by his face that White's QRP is marked out for death.

Or 28. B-Q2, R-B7; 29. B-KB1, RxQRP; 30. BxQKtP, R-KKt7 ch!, and wins. If White had had one tempo more (see note to White's 25th move) this combination would have been impossible. There followed: 28. ....PxB; 2g. KtxP, R—R4; 30. Kt-B2, RxP; 31. Kt-Q4, R-QKt7; 32. P-B5, Kt-B2; 33. PxP, KtxP; 34. Kt-B6, P-Q5, and White resigned.
Illustrates over-protection and also the problem of the isolated QP.
blocks.html: Illustrates over-protection and also the problem of the isolated QP.

blocks.text: P-KB4 is held to be better.
With this exchange, which is anything but obvious, Black plans to win the square Q4 for his Kt.

If P-B5, then P—KKt4. A fight would then take place for possession of the point K4. For example, 8. P-QB5, P-KKt4; 9. Q-K2 (to threaten P-K6 shutting Black in), 9. ....Q-K3; 10. P-KR3, Kt-R3, followed by Kt-B2, or else Kt-QKt1. In either case Black would not stand badly.

We may with a clear conscience regard White's QP as isolated. His weakness (for the end game!) is evident; further Black has in his Q4 a very strong point. As regards any compensating advantage for what we have called his isolated QP White has the outpost station QB5 which will serve some purpose, on the other hand his K5 is of no use to him, as a station for his Kt, I mean. The game is about equal.

It is very questionable whether PxP would not have been better for White than the R move. True his opponent would have had the KKt file and a centrally posted B at Q3, but the K file must not be despised, at any rate as a counter weight. The curious over-protection which is built up in moves 13-18 has been discussed in II. iv, 1, under Diagram CLXVII.
Having consolidated his position, Black passes to the attack, which indeed is not easy to conduct since for one thing objectives are wanting and for another White himself has some attacking chances.

Without question 19. P-QKt4 should have been played here; with the intention of playing when opportunity offered Kt-B5; BxKt, KtPxB. The question now arises, is Black's position strong enough to bear weakening? Two moves in particular come under consideration in answer to 19. P-QKt4, namely 19. ....P-QKt3, and 19. ....P-QKt4. If 19. ....P-QKt3, then 20. Kt-B5! can be played, but after 20. ....BxKt!; 21. KtPxB, P-QB3, Black would stand very well. However, lie must emphatically not accept the Kt. sacrifice as the following combination proves. (See diagram.) 19. P-QKt4!, P-QB3; 20. Kt-B5!, PxKt; 21. KtPxP ch, K-R1? (the return sacrifice Kt—Kt3 was essential); 22. P-B6, Q-K1; 23. R-R4 (threatening RxP ch), Kt-Kt3; 24. P-Q5!!, RxP; 25. RxP ch, KxR; 26. Q-R4 ch, K-Kt1; 27. BxKt, PxB; 28. RxP ch, K-B2; 29. R-Kt7 ch, K-Q1; 30. P-B7 ch!, RxP; 31. R-Kt8 ch, R-B1; 32. RxR ch, and QxQ ch and wins. A true Morphy Combination.

We may quietly note the fact that his over-protected central position is so strong that Black can here without a qualm leave himself unprotected and yet remain master of the situation as he was before, for he is in a position laughingly to evade any enemy combination, be it ever so diabolical.

We have still to show what would happen if Black played 19. ....P-QKt4 in reply to 19. P-QKt4. In this case, too, Black would not fare badly; e.g., 20. R—B6, K—Kt2; 21. Kt-B5 ch, BxKt; 22. RxB, Kt-Kt3; followed by P-QB3, and Black is strong on the White squares.
White has at last spent his fury.
For White would not be able to hold out after 30. PxP, PxP ch; 31. K-B1, QR-KB1 (stronger than R-Kt8 ch).
Note with what surprising ease the Black Rooks are brought into action, a further proof, to my mind, of the enormous vitality of overprotecting pieces.
After RxP, RxR ch the King would be exposed.
Decisive, though so simple and even insipid. It wins the pawns which are so conveniently exposed in the 4th rank.
The Hanham defence. Illustrates combined play on both wings. The fearlessness with which Black is able up to a certain point to ignore his own weakness at Q3 is noticeable.
blocks.html: The Hanham defence. Illustrates combined play on both wings. The fearlessness with which Black is able up to a certain point to ignore his own weakness at Q3 is noticeable.

blocks.text: P-QR4 would have been preferable here.
Black's pawn-mass is now of such a constitution (I mean inner structure), that they must inspire respect. Notice the two-fold possibility of deployment by P-QB4 or, on occasion, P—Q4.
He tries to nip the latent strength of Black's pawns in the bud.
To get out of the way of his vis-a-vis.

White's attempt to pick a quarrel, sit venia verbo, must be regarded as having failed, for Black's PQ3 is easily defendable while the two Bishops in conjunction with the QR file and the threatening diagonal QB1 to KKt5 exercise no mean influence.
A witty defence of the KKtP (QxP??, BxP ch).
The weakness at Q3 is here of but slight importance.
If 24. P-KB4?, then 24. ....PxP; 25. PxP, B—B3, winning a P.
Threatening Kt-R5, and if R-QKt1 then BxKt and BxKP.
The moves now following lead to the occupation of the important files and diagonals.
A weakness has now slowly crystallized out; namely that of White's base. With the Black Kt placed at Q5 the invasion of White's 2nd rank would be decisive.
He has his eye on Q5 but at the same time threatens the K's wing; i.e., by RxKt ch; KtxR, RxKt ch; KxR, Q-B7 ch; K-R3, B-B5! See Diagram CLXXV.
But for the threat just referred to White could perhaps find an adequate defence by 32. Q-Q5, Kt-Q5; 33. P-B4.
But now this move takes place with the win of a tempo.
R-QB1 can no longer be parried, a good example this of how one can devote one's attention to several weaknesses at the same time.
After 34. P-QB3, PxP; 35. PxP, Q-Kt7 ch, the weakness of White's 2nd rank would have been shown up.
or 35. QxQP ch, B-B3; 36. QxQP, R-Q1.
Black in order to maintain his advantage had always to try to combine attack on the K with play in the centre. (Cf. his 40th and 41st moves.)
And now the Q's wing is brought in too.
Now things go easier. 48. Kt-K3, R-Kt6; 49. R-K5, K-B3; 50. R-K8, K-B2; 51. R-K5, R-B3; 52. P-B4, P-Kt6; 53. K-K4, R-K3; 54. RxR, KxR; 55. Kt-Q5, P-Kt4 and White resigned.
A most complicated game in the strategical sense. Lasker manoeuvres on one wing and breaks through on the other. The why and the wherefore of this procedure will be found explained in the notes.
blocks.html: A most complicated game in the strategical sense. Lasker manoeuvres on one wing and breaks through on the other. The why and the wherefore of this procedure will be found explained in the notes.

blocks.text: Black ought to have tried to force White to declare his intentions in the centre; therefore 12. ....BPxP; 13. PxP, B-Kt5.
Intending to invade the centre with Kt-Q5.
The reply to 14. Kt-Q5 would have been 14. ....QR2; 15. KtxB, KtxKt! With the text move Lasker plays for the advantage of the two B's.
Black has consistently kept his end in view, that is to prepare for P-Q4; so now Lasker finds himself forced to play P-Q5 thus blocking his own B. The game now enters a new stage.

Instead of this he should have played P-QB5 followed by Kt—B4. The Kt would then have been well posted and, more importa, wouldnt have a preventive effect, for White was preparing for P-KB4 inter alia.
Black's KKt4 seems now strongly fortified.

If Kt-R4, Black would simply exchange (BxKt, RxB), and the game would then take on a somewhat rigid aspect. Lasker, therefore, wisely avoids Kt-R4 and seeks to preserve whatever latent dynamic force, there is in the position, little though this be.
White intends to play Kt-K3 and wishes to hold the move P—KB4 in readiness should Black play B-Kt4 (Lasker).

Lasker has succeeded in carrying out P-KB4 under circumstances favourable to himself; but there was no direct advantage to be got by the move. However, Black's pieces which have to keep on the look-out against the threat of an invasion by Kt-B5, are less well posted in case of an attack on the Q's wing. And so we may say that Lasker has laid the K's wing under siege in order to bring the enemy pieces out of contact with their own Q's wing, and will now roll up this (left) wing and thus score a double advantage; definite weaknesses are to be created, and in addition his B's are to get room for manoeuvring; for instance, by P-QB4, P-Kt5; B-B2 followed by Q-Q1 and B-QR4.
The decisive error. The right course, as Lasker pointed out in the book of the Congress, was 43. ....BxKt; 44. BxB, QxKtP followed by P-R5 and R-QR1, and Black's game is tenable.
The KtB5 can no longer be driven away by, say, Kt-K2. Black has now evident weaknesses on both wings and Lasker exploits them without any particular trouble.
At last he manages to oust the intruder at his KB4, but meanwhile White is grown too strong on the Q's wing.
There followed: 55. PxP, P—KB4; 56. P-K5, Kt-B3; 57. RxBP, Kt-Kt5; 58. RxB, QxQ; 59. RxQ, PxR; 60. P-Q6, R-QR2; 61. P-K6, R-R3; 62. P-K7, Kt-B3; 63. P-Q7, KtxP; 64. BxKt, Resigns.
This fine game is instructive as illustrating, inter alia, the struggle of united Bishops for open country in which to manoeuvre.
The following, game won a brilliancy prize in the New York tournament, 1927.
Planning P-QR4-R5 and to post the Kt anew at QB4. Black would have done better to exchange Kts on his 9th move. White now gets the advantage.
The prelude to a complicated attacking operation which was the more unexpected since Kt-K4 gave a good game without any effort. But for once I wanted to go in for a combination.
White gets compensation for the QP. Note, inter alia, that Black's Queen side is difficult to develop.

The answer to KtxQP would have been QR—K1!!, by which B-K3 would have been prevented because of BxQBP. Black would then have been quite helpless, and White could have won by, e.g., B-Q2 followed by the doubling of the R's in the K file.
There is a peculiar point in this move.

If, that is to say, 23. ....B-K3, and it is with this parry that White has above all things to reckon, then 24. QxP (threatening BxKt and the win of a piece), 24. ....R-QB1; 25. QR-K1!, and the B must give up the defence of one or other of the R's; on which BxKt would lead to the win of whichever is left defenceless.
The quickest road to the win.
Black's King's wing seems somewhat boxed in, but as compensation his centre is the more mobile.

9. ....P-Q5 would have been bad because of Kt-K4 and the Knight is centrally established. On the other hand 9. ....P-KB3 was well worth consideration. For instance, PxP, BxP and Black controls the centre.

Black wants to score the Kt move as an error, for now the Kt can no longer get to K4. This is, however, a mistake and therefore it would have been much better, to play P-KB3 instead of P-Q5. For example : 10. ....P-KB3; 11. PxP, BxP; 12. P-QB3, P-K4; i3. PxP, KtxP, and Black would not stand badly.

This move, which Black has twice passed over, leads now, thanks to the weakness of his K5 to a result which promises little fruit. The 'prophylactic' defence, 11. ....R-K2; 12. Kt-Kt3, B-KB1; 13. Kt-K4, Kt-Q4 (putting a stop to P-B5), would therefore have deserved the preference.
There was also no true joy to be got out of 12. ....BxP; 13. Kt-Kt3, P-K4; 14. P-B5,
Black seeks to defend his threatened wing from the centre, but this plan should not here have been sufficient to save the situation.
Kt-R5 would have been sharper here. E.g., 16. Kt-R5, Kt-Kt3; 17. BxKt, PxB; 18. Kt-B5 with a winning attack.

With this ingenious diversion Dr. Alekhine succeeds in bringing his opponent's attack to a standstill for some time. The game up to this point is discussed in II. i, § 6, in connexion with 'centralization'.

The position is in a measure cleared up. Black has a passed pawn which it is true is very sick, but very highly insured against death. We mean to say that the Bishop diagonals QB3-KR8 (after B-Q2-B3) and QB4—KKt8 are compensation. Instead of chasing after the dubious win of the pawn it would have been more to the purpose had White gone on with his King side attack; and this by P-Kt5. Neglect of this move throws White back.
White has localised the enemy thrust.
He here misses his opportunity to play P-KKt5, which would have won. For instance: 25. ....PxP; 26. KtxP, RxP; 27. Q-R5; or 25. ....P-B4; 26. Q-R5, PxKt, 27. BxP, etc.
Better, according to H. Wolf, would have been 26. ....P-K7; 27. R-Q1, Q-Kt4 followed by Q-K4.
It happens now as was indicated in the note to the 20th move. White wins the P, but Black keeps the pressure by means of his two Bishops.
With R-KKt1 Black could have increased the pressure.
Pretty but insufficient. True the acceptance of the sacrifice would have been ruinous (33. RxKt, BxR; 34. QxB, Q-B7), but White has a truly startling counter-combination at his disposal.
The point. To strike at once would have been bad, e.g., 34. PxP, K—Kt2; 35. Q-R3, R-KR1; 36. R-Q7 ch, BxR; 37. QxBch, KxP, and White is threatened with mate.
R-KKt1 was imperative. The continuation would have been 35. PxP, K-Kt2; 36. R-Q7 eh, BxR; 37. QxR ch, KxP; 38. B-Q3!, K-R3; 39. Q-R3 ch, K—Kt2; 40. R-KKt1 ch, QxRch!, and the win is still far away.
A simpler win would have been 39. Q-Kt8 ch, K-K2; 40. P-B8 = Q ch, RxQ; 41. R-R7 ch, K-K1; 42. QxB.
The passed pawn's lust to expand!
42. ....Q-B3 would have led not to the exchange of Queens but to the loss of his Queen, namely 43. R-R7 ch, K-K1; 44. B-Kt5.

Illustrates in an instructive manner the connexion between play in the centre on the one hand, and diversions undertaken on the wings on the other. The dependence of a flank attack for success on the 'state of health' of the centre is very clearly brought out. One of four simultaneous consultation games.
blocks.html: Illustrates in an instructive manner the connexion between play in the centre on the one hand, and diversions undertaken on the wings on the other. The dependence of a flank attack for success on the 'state of health' of the centre is very clearly brought out. One of four simultaneous consultation games.

blocks.text: White: E. Andersson, R. Enström, and O. Oeberg.—Black: Nimzowitsch.
Black has now got over the difficulties of the opening.
Obedient to the law that a passed pawn must be blockaded.

It was only reluctantly and after much deliberation that I determined on this diversion on the extreme flank; which looks risky, since the situation in the centre is by no means secure. For one of my leading principles lays down that a flank attack is only justified if the centre is secure. Yet in the present case White cannot force his opponent to play PxKBP, and if he take the KP himself, he gets, it is true, the point K4 (after RxP), but Black by bringing up his reserves can mitigate this danger.
The reserves, see the last note.
Aiming for KKt5 or K5. It will be seen that the consulting players are thoroughly exercised in the art of manoeuvring, and are opponents to be taken seriously.
At last Black proceeds with the attack to which his nth move was the prelude. This, slowness is all to his credit.

This simple strategical retreat reveals my plan of defence. As my system lays down, the ideal aimed at by every operation in a file is the entry into the 7th and 8th ranks. However, here the points of invasion, K7 and K8 are safeguarded, and the RKt3 cannot cooperate since he is deprived of the square K3.

With this retreat a manoeuvre is started which is designed to neutralize the enemy's apparently strong hold on the K file. Less good would have been 27. ....Q-R6 with the idea of getting home safely with the booty by means of 28. ....Q-Q3. thus: 27. ....Q-R6; 28. Kt—K5, Q-Q3; 29. KtxKt, BxKt; 30. Q-KB2, R-K3; 31. R-K5! and White still has drawing chances, whereas the phlegmatic manoeuvre in the text wins.

With this the regrouping R-Q3 and Kt—KB3 is threatened, whereby the R and Kt will have exchanged stations. If White prevents this by 29. Kt-Kt5 (29. ....R-Q3?; 30. QxKt ch and mate next move), White will be undoubtedly strong in the K file, yet the distinctive characteristic of the position, namely the spearhead station of White's Q will prevent, him from taking full advantage of the file. For instance, 29. Kt-Kt5, B-B3; 30. R(Kt)-K3, QxP; or 30. R-K2, Q-B5 (Blockade!); 31. R(Kt)—K3, P-QR4, and wins, for Kt—K6? is impossible because of R-K2, and he has no other effective move in the K file at his disposal. In the game the continuation was:
And now this difficult regrouping manoeuvre (under enemy fire) has been successfully carried out.
A gross mistake, but even after 32. Q-K2, R-K3; 33. Q-Q1, R(Kt)-K2, White's game would have been hopeless.
In the following game two armies out of contact with one another operate in the centre and on a flank. It is interesting to' see how contact is finally established between them.
The innovation introduced by me in 1911 at San Sebastian.
The relationship between the Alekhine Defence (1. P-K4, Kt—KB3) introduced in 1921 and my treatment of the Sicilian will be noted. (Cf., too, Bogoljubow's application of the idea in 1. P-Q4, Kt-QB3.)
White has lost a tempo with his B, on the other hand the Kt at QKt3 is not particularly well placed, so that the B manoeuvre is not to be blamed.
We should have given 7. PxP e.p. the preference.

If the attack planned by this move, namely P—KB4 with P—KKt4 and P-B5 should really prove possible to carry out, this would be a proof of the incorrectness of 8. ....B—B4, and that would be an absurdity. In point of fact the matter stands thus: No particular result is achieved by 11. Kt—K1, and this diversion would better have been abandoned in favour of a systematic utilization of the QB file. For example, 11. B-K3, O-O; 12. R-QB1, followed by P-QR3, P-QKt4 and Kt-Q2-Kt3-B5, when the establishment of an outpost advocated by my system would have been attained.
Cleverly played. The answer to 12. P-KB4 would have been, of course, KtxP; QxKt??, B-QB4. 12. B-K3 would also have been

unfavourable because of 12. ....Kt(Q2)xKP; 13. PxKt, P-Q5; 14. B-Q2, PxKt; 15. BxP, Q-B2, with advantage in position for Black. By aid of the text move (12. B-Kt4) Yates is able in a quite startling manner to make the advance, P-KB4, at which he was aiming.
If 14. ....B-QB4, then 15. P—QKt4 would have been strong.
14. ....PxKt would have also been bad because of BxKt ch, followed by QxKt.

In the face of Black's obvious plan to occupy the central points, White should, by himself Centralizing, have disputed them with his opponent, thus: 17. Q-K2 (intending B-K3), 17. ....Kt-Q4; 18. B-B3, Q-B4; 19. B-Q2, Kt(Q2)-Kt3; 20. R-QB1, Q-K2, and White has more of the centre than Black. And even if such a 'more' were not attainable, what matter! Even in this case White ought to have fought for it. As it is a just punishment now overtakes him.
Forced, for if B-B3, then Kt-KB4 with a further gain of terrain in the centre; moreover, there would then be a mating threat in the air, namely P-R5 and Kt-Kt6 ch.
Making room for the Kt at Q2, which is aiming for Q4 via QKt3.

This move in conjunction with the one next following leads to a decentralization of one of his R's, and so to a defect in his position which has been so harmoniously constructed. On the other hand the continuation 23. ....O-O-O! held out the promise of untroubled harmony; for after 24. ....K-QKt1 and 25. ....P-PKt3 nothing stood in the way of employing the two R's centrally, e.g., 26. ....R-Q2; 27. ....R-QB1.

However, 23. ....B-KKt5 seems to be still better. For instance, 24. BxB, PxB; 25. QxP, RxP; 26. QxKKtP, O-O-O; 27. KxR, QxR; 28. Kt-Q3, Q-K7, and Black must win. Or, lastly, it was also possible to combine the two plans, thus: 23. ....O-O-O; 24. B-R3 and now 24. ....B-Kt5. If then perhaps 25. R—QB1 ch, K—Kt1; 26. B-QB5, then 26. ....QxB; 27. RxQ, BxQ; 28. RxB, R-QB1 with a victorious incursion via the QB file.

Interesting, for when all is said and done. Black's position, centralized even to the extent that it is, can support an adventurous raid; yet 24. ....O-O with P-KKt3 and KR-Q1 was certainly more correct.

Black's structure suffers under an inner discord. The position of the cut off R makes a mating attack seem desirable; but the disposition of the rest of the army is rather directed towards the end game, in which the KtQ4 would have enormous effect, while the white squares would be in Black's undisputed possession.
To draw the sting of the threat Q-R7 and Q-Kt8 ch, the R runs away betimes. Black has in fact to manoeuvre very cautiously.
33. ....KtxKt ch.; 34. RxKt, RxR; 35. QxR, P-KKt3, would not have been good because of 36. P-B5.
He does not mind the threat, has his eye, moreover, on his QB4 (Q-B4).
As the detachments which have been cut off cannot get back to the army, the latter comes to them.
If 37. KtxR, then RxRP ch and mate in two moves.
Again threatening mate, this time by RxKtP ch, etc.
For this game I was awarded the special prize of £ 10, 'for the best played game' in the tournament.
There follow five games of historical interest.
A most instructive game from A to Z, one which I regard as the first in which my new philosophy of the centre was exhibited. See I. ix, § 5, P. 126.
blocks.html: A most instructive game from A to Z, one which I regard as the first in which my new philosophy of the centre was exhibited. See I. ix, § 5, P. 126.

blocks.text: See note to this move in Game No. 19.
Since White still delays PxP, Black intends to force his hand with R-QB1. The right course was 6. ....PxP; 7. PxP and thus to pass into quite other channels. See Games Nos. 19 and 20.
Black swells in triumph and throws himself hungrily on the last remaining member of the once so proud chain-family, to destroy him. His war cry is 'Room for the KP!' But it happens quite otherwise.
In order to be able tox provide his K5 with an enduring defence.
9. Q-K2 would also have been a defence, but no enduring one, for there would follow 9. ....PxP; 10. KtxP, KtxKt; 11. QxKt, K-KB3 and the blockading Q at K5 will be easily driven away.
Again we have the exchange operation which we have so often discussed; this time, however, it is not really justified, for the new blockader, the BK5, proves to be a stout fellow.
For the otherwise desirable B-B3 would fail against 13. Q-R5 ch, P KKt3; 14. BxP ch, PxB; 15. QxP ch, K-K2; 16. BxB ch, KtxB; 17. Q-Kt7 ch.
That the win of a pawn by 13. Q-B2?, O-O, etc. is a snare, has been pointed out under Diagram CVII.
The blockading forces are to be reinforced by the Kt.
14. ....B-QKt4 would yield little profit for 15. B-Q4, Q-R3; l6. BxB, QxB; 17. Kt-Kt5, would win a pawn.
That 15. B-Q4 would be premature has been pointed out under Diagram CVII.

The immobility of the KP is now greater than ever. White has utilized his resources very economically. The possibility of a successful occupation of the points Q4, K5, hung on a hair, on taking minute advantage of the terrain, i.e., of the points Q4, K5, QB2, and K2.
In order to force Black's QB who also has his eye on the KR4 to come to a decision.
30. ....K-Kt1; 31. P-QR3, K-B1; 32. B-R4, B-K1; 33. B-B5, Q-Q5; 34. QxQ, PxQ; 35. RxR, KxR; 36. B-Q3, IC-Q3; 37. BxKt, PxB; 38. P-KR4, Resigns.

Of special interest historically as being the first game in which what has been called the 'Ideal Queen's Gambit' was played, where Black forgoes altogether the occupation of the centre by his pawns. It was played in the all-Russian Tournament in Petrograd, 1913.
blocks.html: Of special interest historically as being the first game in which what has been called the 'Ideal Queen's Gambit' was played, where Black forgoes altogether the occupation of the centre by his pawns. It was played in the all-Russian Tournament in Petrograd, 1913.

blocks.text: In answer to 3. P-QB4 I had intended P-QKt3. The point Q4 is to remain permanently unoccupied.
Black has the two Bishops, and in what follows is concerned to keep them.
In order after P-Q3 not to be exposed to the move P—K5, which would open the game.
The mobility of White's centre must be rated as very slight, for any thrust would be intercepted without any trouble; e.g., 12. P—K5, P-Q4!; or 12. P-Q5, P-K4!

A strategical device which, the Hyper-modernist may care to note, makes its appearance here. I mean the continuity of an attack directed against a pawn-mass. This is to be understood thus: the threatened advance must first have its sting drawn (in this game this was done by Q-K2). It is only when this has happened that we may regard the mass as semi-mobile, and attack it; for only those objects which have been made immobile should be chosen as a target.
14. Kt—Q2 was to be considered. For instance, 14. ....BxRP; 15. P-KB4 with definite chances.
If 20. Kt-Kt3 then 20. ....P-QKt5 and if 21. P-QB4, B-K1 with the superior game.
Now the Bishops assert their rights.
Threatens complete paralysis by R(R1)-R7, since R-Kt1 is then impossible because of RxR ch and R-R8.

The win is still some considerable way off. In what follows Black manoeuvres against the QBP, but also keeps before himself the possibility of an incursion of his K at KKt6, as for instance at the 70th move. However, this by itself would not suffice, Black has also still to play out the duel on the K's wing with his pawn-majority, and in doing so his position will become broken up, and with all this the QBP is not to be joked with.
The point KKt6 now looks ripe for an invasion by Black.
At last the fitting moment has arrived.
Now the King threatens to journey to his KKt6.

This game aroused lively interest at the time, and the idea was tried at the same tournament by other masters though with indifferent success. I continued my studies of the opening, and employed it the next year, 1914, in the Great Petrograd Tournament, and against Janowski and Bernstein. The first 18 moves of the former game were given and discussed in II. ii. § 2. Against Bernstein (White) the game ran: 1. P-Q4, Kt-KB3; 2. Kt-KB3, P-K3; 3. P-QB4, P-QKt3; 4. Kt-QB3, B-Kt2; 5. P-K3, B-QKt5; 6. Q-Kt3, Q-K2; 7. P-QR3, BxKt ch; 8. QxB, B-Q3; 9. P-QKt4, QKt-Q2; (Black now has an excellent game; the mobility of the White centre is slight, and the diagonal QKt2 to K5 is an important asset.) 10. B-Kt2 P-QR4 (good enough, but Kt-K5 and P-KB4 was preferable); 11. B-K2, PxP; 12. PxP, RxR ch; 13. BxR, O-O; 14. O-O, Kt-K5; 15. Q-B2, P-KB4; 16. Kt-Q2, KtxKt (16. ....P—QB4 with its hyper-modern savour would seem to be more in keeping here.) 17. QxKt, R-QR1; 18. B-QB3, Q-K1 (with 18. ....Kt-KB3 in order to anticipate P-Q5, Black's game would still have been good); 19. P-Q5!, P-K4 (PxP?, B-KB3); 20. P-KB4, B-B1; and, after a sequence of highly dramatic complications, the game ended in a draw.
In the same tournament Alekhine adopted my innovation—the 'Ideal Queen's Gambit'—and with success.
Being the first game in which the thesis of the relative harmlessness of the 'pawn-roller' was stated.
blocks.html: Being the first game in which the thesis of the relative harmlessness of the 'pawn-roller' was stated.

blocks.text: This set Spielmann thinking. After some minutes I raised my eyes from the board and saw that my dear old companion in arms was quite disconcerted. He looked at the Kt, now confidently, now suspiciously, and after much hesitation gave up the possible chase started by P—K5 and played the more circumspect Kt-QB3. Next year I tried 2. ....Kt—KB3 on Schlechter, and in the Book of the Congress we find the following note to this move by Tarrasch: 'Not good, since the Kt is at once driven away, but Herr Nimzowitsch goes his own road in the openings, one, however, which cannot be recommended to the public.'

Ridicule can do much, for instance embitter the existence of young talents; but one thing is not given to it, to put a stop permanently to the incursion of new and powerful ideas. The old dogmas, such as the ossified teaching on the centre, the worship of the open game, and in general the whole formalistic conception of the game, who bothers himself to-day about these? The new ideas, however, those supposed by-ways, not to be recommended to the public, these are become to-day highways, on which great, and small move freely in the consciousness of absolute security.

My game against Schlethter ran as follows: 1, P-K4, P-QB4; 2. Kt—KB3, Kt-KB3; 3. P-K5, Kt-Q5; 4. P-Q4. Why, asks Dr. Tarrasch, should not P-QB4 be played here? The Black Kt would then certainly be driven on to unfavourable squares. Alas, no; even in the case of 1. P-K4, Kt—KB3 (Alekhine's defence); the effect of driving the Kt by 2. P-K5, Kt-Q4; 3. P-QB4, Kt-Kt3; 4. P-Q4 is merely to compromise White's game.

In my game against Schlechter the continuation was : 4. ....PxP; 5. QxP, P-K3; 6. B-QB4, Kt-QB3; 7. Q-K4, P-Q3!; 8. PxP (or 8. BxKt, PxB; 9. QxP, PxP; with two B's and a compact pawn majority), Kt-KB3; 9. Q—KR4, BxP; 10. Kt-QB3, Kt-K4!; and Black obtained a certain freedom for manoeuvring in the middle of the board.
To return to my game with Spielmann.
What now follows is play against the hanging pawns which will soon come into existence.
This exchange in conjunction with Kt-QKt5 is the point of the proceedings started by 9. ....Q-B2.
The hanging pawns, which come under heavy fire, prove, however, in the end to have a lot of vigour. The game is about equal.
19. P-B5, BxKt; 20. PxB would have led to a draw.
With his B thus posted Black's advantage is clear.
White cannot well give up the QB file; if, however, 28. R-B3 then 28. ....P-KR4; 29. P-KR4, RxP.
A passed pawn plus a mating attack, a wicked affair.
But he was lost whatever he did.
This being the first game in which my idea of a sacrifice for the sole purpose of establishing a blockade was illustrated.
blocks.html: This being the first game in which my idea of a sacrifice for the sole purpose of establishing a blockade was illustrated.

blocks.text: The over-protection of the strategically important PK5.

This was no ordinary pawn sacrifice for the attack. Its motive was simply and exclusively this, to maintain the point K5, in order to use it as' a base for a blockading action. We know this motive in draughts, where a man is sacrificed in order to make it possible to lock up an enemy majority by our minority. To have translated this idea to the field of chess was a revolutionary act.
This, too, is no attacking move in the ordinary sense; its meaning is: 'Get away from the Key Square K5.'
This move, which throws open all lines of approach to his opponent, he has got to make in order to give himself air; and with it White's attack first appears in evidence.
20. B—KB5 with a strong attack, and White won on the 44th move.

My game against Leonhardt (Black) in the same tournament took much the same course: 1. P-K4, P-K3; 2. P-Q4, P—Q4; 3. P-K5, P-QB4; 4. Kt—KB3 (later I discovered the still more revolutionary Q-Kt4), see No. 50. 4. ....Q-Kt3; 5. B-Q3, PxP; 6. O-O, Kt-QB3; 7. P-QR3, KKt—K2; 8. P-QKt4, Kt-Kt3; 9. R-K1, B-K2; 10. B-Kt2, P—QR4. Black now has to give up the pawn again; after 10. ....P-QR3!, we should have had the state of affairs we have discussed, namely pawn plus vs. a cramping policy.
The same strategical device appeared in a particularly plastic shape in a game played in 1913, when the position shown in the diagram was reached.

The game continued 19. ....P-QKt4!!; Black sacrifices a P in order to exchange White's KB, after which the blockade of White's position by Kt—KB4 will become effective. There followed, 20. BxP, R(QR)-QKt1; 21. B-K2, Kt-Kt3; (more precise was Kt—Kt2 at once; for if P—KR5, then Kt-Kt3, followed by the forced exchange at B5 [Kt—B5, BxKt], and finally by the occupation of his KB4 by the Kt, with a positional winning advantage for Black). 22. K-Q1 (he could have saved himself by 22. BxKt, Kt—B5; 23. Q-B2, KtxRP; 24. Q-Q2); ' 22. ....Kt-B5; 23. BxKt, RxB; 24. R-Kt5, Kt-Kt2; 25. P-KR5, Kt-B4; 26. PxP, BPxP; and Black won without difficulty.

From a match; the first game in which appears my idea of a pawn sacrifice in the opening, not to obtain an attack, but merely, with gain of a tempo, to overprotect a strategical point with a view to cramping the enemy forces.

blocks.text: White's plan is now clear. He has given up a pawn, careless when, if ever, he recover it provided his PK5 is maintained as an instrument to cramp Black's game. There is no idea of attack in 9. P-KR4, its object is solely to pave the way to the removal of some of the pressure on the PK5. The pawn sacrifice clearly comes within the category of sacrifice for the sake of blockade, cf. game No. 49.
B-B4 was essential here so as to leave the KB square free for the Kt to retreat to after P-R5.

White could, of course, have won the exchange here by 12. P-R5, Kt-K2; 13. Kt-Kt5, R-K1; 14. Kt-B7, R—Kt1; 15. Kt-Q6 ch; but with his undeveloped Q side and his unprotected PR5 he would have had some difficulties to contend with. The text move is the logical continuation.

Rather better was 12. ....K—Kt1; e.g., i3. P-QB3!, PxP; 14. KtxP, KtxQKtP; 15. PxKt, QxKt; 16. B-K3, QxB; 17. BxP ch, K-B1; 18. KR-QB1 ch, B-B3; 19. P-Kt5!, QxP; 20. Kt-Q4 with complications, which, of course. White, had he been so minded, could have avoided by simply playing 13. B-QKt2.
The Q is well placed here.

His only move. It will be noted that the over-protector, the RK1, now has the QB file opened for him without any trouble to himself. In order to avoid loss of material Black has to submit to a curious regrouping of his forces.
The Q finds herself in a position to which as a rule she would only be consigned in a problem.

diagrams.label: Diagram I
diagrams.caption: The Frontier Line
diagrams.context:
The line shown on Diagram I we call the frontier; 'line' is of course to be taken in its mathematical, not in its chess sense. The point marked on Diagram II is the mid-point of the board, again naturally in its mathematical sense. The mid-point is easy to find, it is the point of intersection of the long diagonals.

§ 1. By development is to be understood the strategic advance of the troops to the frontier line.

diagrams.label: Diagram II
diagrams.caption: The Mid.-Point The Small Square is the centre
diagrams.context:
§ 1. By development is to be understood the strategic advance of the troops to the frontier line.

The process is analogous to the advance on the outbreak of a war. Both armies seek to reach the frontier as quickly as possible in order to penetrate into enemy territory.

diagrams.label: Diagram III
diagrams.caption: Typical win of a tempo
diagrams.context:
§ 3. To be ahead in development is the ideal to be aimed at.

If I were running a race with someone, it would be, to say the least, inopportune were I to throw away valuable time by rubbing, say, a smut off my nose, although I must not be considered as blaming that operation in itself. If, however, I can induce my opponent to waste time by some similar action I should then get an advantage in development over him. The repeated moving to and fro of the same piece would be described as an action of this kind. Accordingly we force our opponent to lose time if we make a developing move which at the same time attacks one of his pieces which he has already moved. (See Diagram III. ) This very typical situation arises after 1. P-K4, P-Q4; 2. PxP, QxP; 3. Kt-QB3.

§ 4. Exchange with resulting gain of tempo.

diagrams.label: Diagram IV
diagrams.caption: White to move. The exchange is made in order to entice the recapturing piece on to a compromised square
diagrams.context:
The moves just given show in the compactest form a manoeuvre which we may call a compound one. For why (see Diagram IV ) do we take the QP? (2. PxP). The answer is to entice the piece which recaptures it on to a square exposed to attack. This was the first part of the manoeuvre. The second (3. Kt-QB3) consisted in the utilization of the Queen's position which is in a certain sense compromised.

The compound manoeuvre which we have just outlined is one of the greatest value to the student, and we proceed to give a few more examples. 1. P-Q4, P-Q4; 2. P-QB4, Kt-KB3; 3. PxP!. And now two variations follow. If 3. ....QxP, then 4. Kt-QB3; and if 3. ....KtxP; 4. P-K4; so that in either case White with his 4th move will have made a developing move of full value, which Black will be forced to answer by wandering about. But perhaps the beginner may say in his heart: Why should Black recapture? Many a skillful business man displays in chess an altogether unnatural delicacy of feeling; he does not recapture. But the master unfortunately knows that he is under compulsion, there's no remedy for it, he must recapture, else the material balance in the centre would be disturbed. It follows from the fact that this is compulsory that the capture retards, for the moment at any rate, the enemy's development, except in the case when the recapture can be made with what is at the same time a developing move. A further example:— 1. P-K4, P-K4; 2. P-KB4, Kt-KB3; 3. PxP!, KtxP; forced, otherwise Black would be a pawn down with no equivalent for it. 4. Kt-KB3! (to prevent Q-R5), Kt-QB3; 5. P-Q3 (the logical complement of the exchange PxP), 5. ....Kt-B4; 6. P-Q4, Kt-K5; 7. P-Q5, and after 7. ....Kt-Kt1 White will have the opportunity of gaining more tempi by 8. B-Q3 or 8. QKt-Q2. The latter contingency must be carefully weighed. The exchange of the time-devouring Kt at K5 for the new-born Kt at Q2 means loss of tempo for Black, since with the disappearance of the Knight there will vanish also the tempi consumed by him; that is to say there will be nothing on the board to show for them. (When a farmer loses a sucking pig through illness, he mourns not only the little pig but also the good food he has gambled on it: the bran, etc.)

An intermezzo is possible in the manoeuvre: exchange with gain of tempo.
